pedagogy.summary: At 10-11 this is the capstone of repeated reasoning: abstracting an algebraic rule from a run of cases and VERIFYING it. The child builds the interior-angle-sum rule (n−2)×180° from triangle/quadrilateral/pentagon, writes the nth-term rule of a linear sequence to predict any term, and generalises structural facts — always testing the generalisation on a specific case. CCSS MP8's own high examples live here: abstracting slope into (y−2)/(x−1)=3, and spotting the cancelling pattern in (x−1)(x+1), (x−1)(x²+x+1)… to reach a general formula. Teaching should organise cases in a table so the regularity is visible, press for the general rule in symbols, and demand a verifying case — the difference between a conjecture and a checked generalisation.
bestPractices: Tabulate a family of cases (polygon sides vs angle sum; position vs term) so the constant step and the offset are visible before the rule is written
Move from 'what's the pattern?' to 'write the rule for the nth/any case' in words then symbols
Always verify a stated generalisation on a fresh specific case (test (n−2)×180 on a hexagon) before trusting it
Decompose the geometric case (split a polygon into n−2 triangles) so the rule is explained, not just fitted
keyRepresentations: Polygon triangulation (an n-gon splits into n−2 triangles)
Position-vs-term tables and the nth-term expression
Linear-sequence graphs/number lines showing constant difference and offset
Algebra tiles / area models for operation-property generalisations
commonMisconceptions: Uses a term-to-term rule and cannot produce an nth-term rule for a far term
Assumes direct proportion — e.g. angle sum is n×180° or the 20th term is 20×(first term) — ignoring the −2 offset / start value
States a generalisation but never verifies it on a specific case, so errors go uncaught
Fits a rule to the given cases that fails to generalise (a pattern that works for 3, 4, 5 sides but wasn't reasoned from structure)

learn.summary: For ages 10-11, this is the capstone of 'look for and express regularity in repeated reasoning': abstract a general algebraic rule from a run of specific cases AND verify it on a fresh case. Learners build the interior-angle-sum rule (n−2)×180° from triangle/quadrilateral/pentagon, write the nth-term rule of a linear sequence to predict any term, and generalise structural facts about operations — each time testing the generalisation on a specific case. The core discrimination is twofold: (a) capturing the −2 offset / start value instead of assuming direct proportion (n×180°, or 20th term = 20×first term), and (b) treating verification on a new case as a reflex, not an afterthought. Teaching should tabulate the cases so the constant step and offset are visible, press for the rule in words then symbols, decompose the geometric case so the rule is explained rather than curve-fitted, and always demand a verifying case.

activities.title: Polygon angle-sum explorer: build, tabulate, abstract, verify
feedback: If the learner writes n×180° (e.g. 6×180 = 1080° for a hexagon), triangulate the hexagon together and count: there are 4 triangles, not 6. Test the n×180 rule against the known pentagon (it gives 900°, not 540°) and watch it fail — a convex n-gon triangulated from one vertex always yields exactly n−2 triangles, so the sum is (n−2) lots of 180°, not n.

If the learner states a rule and stops, do not confirm it; ask 'does it give the pentagon's 540°? Now test the hexagon, which you held back and did not use to build the rule.' Make the verifying case a required step every time.
If the learner reaches (n−2)×180° with the triangle reasoning and checks the hexagon at 720°, affirm both the structural justification AND the check as the target — the formula alone is not enough.
activities.rationale: Tabulating a family of cases makes the constant step (+180°) and the offset (−2) visible before the rule is written; decomposing the polygon into n−2 triangles explains the rule structurally so it generalises instead of merely fitting 3,4,5 sides; demanding a fresh verifying case separates a conjecture from a checked generalisation.
sourceClaims: Pupils should recognise and use mathematical structure to generalise and should reason about why relationships hold, using representations that reveal the structure
learnerActions: Start with a triangle (angle sum 180°). Add one side at a time to make a quadrilateral, then a pentagon (convex shapes); for each, split the polygon into triangles by drawing diagonals from one vertex. Keep the hexagon back as a fresh test case.
Record in a running table: number of sides, number of triangles, and angle sum. Notice the sum climbs by a steady +180° each time while the triangle count stays at (sides − 2).

Explain WHY: in a convex polygon, from one vertex you can reach the n−3 non-adjacent vertices by diagonals, so an n-sided polygon splits into exactly n−2 triangles, and its angle sum is (n−2) lots of 180° — reason the rule from the structure, don't just fit it to the numbers.
Write the general rule in words ('two fewer than the number of sides, times 180°') then in symbols: (n−2)×180°.

Verify on a case you did not build the rule from: test a hexagon — (6−2)×180° = 720° — and check it matches the measured/added angles. Then stretch it: a decagon (10 sides, 1440°) and a 100-gon — does it still make sense?
activities.intendedInsight: The angle sum is (n−2)×180° BECAUSE the polygon decomposes into n−2 triangles — a rule explained by structure, and confirmed by testing a new polygon rather than trusted on faith.

activities.title: nth-term rule tester for a linear sequence
feedback: If the learner extends the sequence step by step instead of writing a rule, tabulate position against term and ask for the 100th term — continuing by hand becomes impractical, motivating the nth-term rule.

If the learner writes 20 × (first term) for the 20th term, test that rule against a known term (does term = position × first term give the 2nd term correctly? 2×5 = 10, but the 2nd term is 9) and see it fail; locate the missing offset.

If the learner writes 4n + 1, checks it against the listed terms and then confirms it on a fresh term such as the 5th (21), affirm that testing a case not used to build the rule is how you move from a conjecture to a checked generalisation.
activities.rationale: Position-vs-term tables reveal the difference and offset; requiring prediction of a far term forces a genuine nth-term rule rather than term-to-term iteration; checking the rule against a listed term builds verification into the habit and exposes the direct-proportion misconception.
sourceClaims: Pupils should recognise and use mathematical structure to generalise and should reason about why relationships hold, using representations that reveal the structure
learnerActions: Take a linear sequence such as 5, 9, 13, 17, … and tabulate position (1, 2, 3, 4) against term so the constant difference (+4) and the start value are visible.
Move from the term-to-term rule ('add 4') to a position-to-term rule: difference × n + offset. For 5, 9, 13, 17 this is 4n + 1.
Predict a far term you cannot easily count to — the 20th term (81) and the 100th term (401) — using the rule, not step-by-step continuation.

Verify: first check your rule reproduces every listed term (e.g. the 4th term should give 4×4+1 = 17), then test a fresh case not used to build it — extend the sequence by one step to get the 5th term (21) and check that 4×5+1 = 21. If a conjectured rule breaks any term, it is wrong — fix it.
Explain why direct proportion fails here: the 20th term is NOT 20 × the first term, because the sequence does not pass through zero at position zero (the rule 4n+1 gives 1 at n=0, not 0).
activities.intendedInsight: A general nth-term rule lets you jump to any term directly, and the offset (start value) matters — direct proportion from the first term is a classic error that verification against a known term catches.

activities.title: Generalise a structural fact and find the case that disproves a false rule
feedback: If a learner cannot say what the −2 corresponds to, return to the triangulation of a convex polygon: from one vertex you can draw diagonals only to the n−3 non-adjacent vertices, which splits the polygon into exactly n−2 triangles (a hexagon gives 4). Each side not touching the chosen vertex is the base of one triangle; the 2 sides that meet at the chosen vertex do not get a triangle of their own, which is where the −2 comes from.
If a learner accepts a false rule, ask them to find one polygon (or one sequence term) where it breaks; a single counterexample is enough to reject it.
Affirm a response that states the rule, grounds it in structure, and can name a disproving case for a false alternative.
activities.rationale: Reasoning about why a relationship holds (not just that it fits cases) is what makes a generalisation reliable; practising counterexample selection trains the verification habit the assessment targets. Algebra tiles/area models are offered as optional representations that may make the structure visible for simpler products.
sourceClaims: MP8's advanced examples: abstracting slope into an equation from repeated checks, and noticing the cancelling regularity across (x−1)(x+1), (x−1)(x²+x+1)… to reach a general formula — generalising from repeated reasoning
Pupils should recognise and use mathematical structure to generalise and should reason about why relationships hold, using representations that reveal the structure
learnerActions: Generalise an operation property with a reason, e.g. 'any whole number m divided by a non-zero whole number n can be written as the fraction m/n, so dividing by n gives a denominator of n (before any simplifying)' — state it, then justify why it holds, not just that it works on examples.

Explore the cancelling regularity in products like (x−1)(x+1), (x−1)(x²+x+1), … and describe the general pattern that emerges; an area model or algebra tiles may help visualise the simpler binomial product (x−1)(x+1), but are harder to apply to the cubic case, so treat them as an optional aid rather than a required method.

Practise verification-by-counterexample: given a false claim such as 'a polygon's angle sum is n×180°', name the specific polygon that shows it is wrong and state what it gives versus the true value (e.g. pentagon: rule gives 900°, truth is 540°).
Answer the discriminating prompt: 'Why n−2 and not n — what does the −2 correspond to in the shape?'
activities.intendedInsight: Generalising means stating a rule, justifying why it holds from structure, and being able to produce the single case that would disprove a false version — all three are part of mathematical reasoning.

constraints: Verification is not optional: every stated generalisation must be tested on a fresh specific case before it is trusted. Do not let a learner stop at a rule, and do not simply confirm a rule for them — ask for the verifying case.
Guard against the direct-proportion misconception explicitly: n×180° for angle sums and 20×(first term) for the 20th term are the key errors to surface and refute, not avoid.

The rule must be reasoned from structure (a convex n-gon triangulated from one vertex is n−2 triangles), not merely curve-fitted to 3, 4, 5 sides; a pattern that happens to fit the given cases but wasn't reasoned may not generalise.

A static triangulation diagram or a pre-filled table is a useful reference for showing the decomposition, but by itself it does not let the learner conjecture a rule and test it on a new case — pair any static display with an actual conjecture-and-check task.

An interactive explorer or a well-designed quiz (deriving the rule, finding a far term, and selecting the case that disproves a false rule) can each be used during teaching, not only for assessment; choose by what the learner needs to do, not by assuming one medium alone can teach generalisation.

3D representation is unlikely to be needed here because polygon angle sums, linear sequences and operation properties are flat/symbolic; it may add handling load rather than insight for this specific content. This is a scoped judgement about this topic, not a universal or verified claim about 3D.
Area models/algebra tiles are an optional representation whose fit is strongest for simple binomial products; do not present them as a verified or required method for the cubic cancelling pattern.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and the legacy 'verified' flags were not independently re-checked.

Self-audit of the examples used: triangle 180°, quadrilateral 360°, pentagon 540°, hexagon (6−2)×180° = 720°, decagon (10−2)×180° = 1440° — all consistent with (n−2)×180°. The n×180 distractor gives pentagon 900° and hexagon 1080°, correctly shown as wrong. Sequence 5,9,13,17 has rule 4n+1: 4th term 4×4+1 = 17 ✓, 20th term 81, 100th term 401 — consistent.

The legacy 'possible'/'poor' fit entries carried universal-sounding claims (a tap-to-reveal 'cannot' let the child conjecture; 'open talk gives nothing to test'; '3D adds load, not insight'). These have been softened to scoped, qualified observations with stated affordances/limits in the constraints; catalog fit rankings and quiz-step vocabulary were removed.

The operation-property example was tightened to 'any whole number m divided by n can be written as the fraction m/n'; the exact source wording ('dividing by n always gives a denominator of n') was looser and reviewers may wish to confirm the intended statement.

The original source listed an algebra-tile/area-model representation for operation-property generalisations and for the (x−1)(x+1)… cancelling pattern; the applicability of area models to the polynomial-factoring (cubic) example is plausible but not established by the cited sources and is now scoped as optional and reviewable.

probeDeeper: Ask 'why n−2 and not n — what does the −2 correspond to in the shape?' to test whether the rule is reasoned from structure or curve-fitted

Counterexample tuned to this topic: 'a classmate says the angle sum is n×180° — which polygon would show that's wrong, and what does it give versus the true value?' to probe verification by counterexample
Ask 'use your rule to find the angle sum of a decagon (10 sides), then a 100-gon — does it still make sense?' to test generality and reasonableness
Ask 'write the rule for the nth term of 5, 9, 13, 17… and prove it gives the 4th term correctly' to link generalisation with verification
assess.correctAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for (n−2)×180° reached by reasoning (each extra side adds 180° / an n-gon is n−2 triangles), and a verification on the hexagon giving (6−2)×180 = 720°. The reasoned rule AND the check are the target, not the formula alone.

errorPatterns.pattern: Assumes direct proportion — writes the angle sum as n×180° (or the 20th term as 20×the first term), ignoring the −2 offset / start value
errorPatterns.nextMove: Triangulate the polygon to show it is n−2 triangles, not n; test the n×180 rule against the known pentagon and see it fail
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child gives 6×180 = 1080° for a hexagon, or scales the first term by the position

errorPatterns.pattern: Uses a term-to-term rule and cannot produce a general nth-term rule for a far term
errorPatterns.nextMove: Tabulate position against term so the position-to-term relationship (difference×n + offset) is visible; ask for the 100th term
errorPatterns.revealedBy: For the linked sequence task the child extends step-by-step rather than writing an nth-term rule

errorPatterns.pattern: States a generalisation but never verifies it on a specific case, so a wrong rule goes uncaught
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do NOT simply confirm the rule; require a verifying case every time ('does it give the pentagon's 540°?') so checking becomes automatic
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child gives a rule and stops; when asked to test the hexagon, hasn't thought to

responseLevels.gap: Spots '+180°' or 'add 4' but writes no general rule, or uses n×180 / direct proportion, and does not verify
responseLevels.full: Abstracts (n−2)×180° (and nth-term rules) with a structural justification and verifies on a new case, catching direct-proportion errors — generalising AND checking unprompted
responseLevels.partial: Produces a general rule when prompted (often needing the table) but omits the offset reasoning or does not test it on a fresh case

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A triangle's angles add to 180°, a quadrilateral's to 360°, a pentagon's to 540°. What is the rule for the angle sum of a polygon with n sides? How did you get it — and test your rule on a hexagon.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Spotting '+180° each time' is easy; the discriminating parts are (a) capturing the −2 offset in a general rule rather than n×180, and (b) verifying on a new case. A child reasoning correctly explains the n−2 triangles and checks the hexagon; a child reasoning incorrectly writes n×180 (direct proportion) or states a rule without testing it.
